edition.sessionCovered: Fri, Nov 6 (NFP blowout 165K vs 65K est · Gold slides to $4,060 on margin calls · BTC $75,943 · Brent flat $98)
edition.stripNote: Sat 7 Nov. NFP blowout +165K beats 65K consensus — unemployment falls to 4.1%. Gold drops to $4,060 on margin calls and hike fears. Brent $98 — flat on week's tanker-attack volatility. BTC stabilises near $75,943. S&P 500 up 0.3% but down 2.7% on the week.
edition.scoreboardCaption: Fri 6 Nov vs Thu 5 Nov close. Ranked best to worst.
edition.commodleHint: October _____ surprised at +165K, more than double consensus, but failed to lift risk assets as rate-hike fears dominated

overview: October nonfarm payrolls shocked markets on Friday with a 165,000 gain — more than double the 65,000 consensus — while the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1% from 4.2%. Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% month-over-month and 3.1% year-over-year. Rather than lifting risk assets, the hot data reinforced expectations for a December rate hike, with CME FedWatch probability holding near 78%. The S&P 500 eked out a 0.3% gain to 7,377 — a modest bounce from Thursday's 4.4% plunge — while the Nasdaq Composite rallied 1.1% as chip stocks staged a partial 3.5% recovery from the prior session's 12% collapse. But on the week the S&P 500 fell 2.7%, its worst since the April 2025 tariff shock. The Dow slipped 0.5% as financials and healthcare gave back post-midterm gains. Treasury yields firmed: the 10-year rose 2 basis points to 4.86% and the 2-year climbed 5 basis points to 4.52%. The University of Michigan preliminary November consumer sentiment index came in at 51.0, above the 48.0 consensus, adding to the hawkish data mix.

Gold was the day's notable casualty, dropping 0.9% to approximately $4,060 per ounce as the hot jobs print triggered margin calls and reinforced rate-hike expectations — a reversal of Thursday's safe-haven bid. Goldman Sachs cut its year-end 2026 gold target from $4,650 to $4,150. Silver slipped 0.8% to $51.90. Brent crude held flat near $98.32, essentially consolidating after a wild week in which it swung from $105+ to $94 to $98 on the midterm-peace-then-tanker-attack whiplash — down 13% for the week, its steepest weekly drop since March 2020. WTI edged up to $90.83. Bitcoin stabilised near $75,943, roughly flat, after Thursday's $1 billion liquidation cascade, but remains approximately 40% below its all-time high. Platinum rallied 1.1% to $1,538, its best weekly gain since August at nearly 8%, while palladium held near $1,023. The dollar index gained 0.76% to 102.32, supported by the hot labour data. October CPI on Tuesday is now the key catalyst for the December Fed decision.

watchItems.title: NFP blowout: 165K jobs cement December hike expectations
watchItems.text: October nonfarm payrolls rose 165,000 — more than double the 65,000 consensus — while the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1% from 4.2%. Average hourly earnings climbed 3.1% year-over-year. The strong data reinforced CME FedWatch pricing of a 78% probability of a 25 basis-point hike at the December 8–9 FOMC meeting. The report prompted Goldman Sachs to cut its year-end gold target from $4,650 to $4,150. Treasury yields rose across the curve, with the 10-year at 4.86%. October CPI data on Tuesday is the next pivotal release.

watchItems.title: Gold slides on margin calls — Goldman cuts target to $4,150
watchItems.text: Gold fell 0.9% to approximately $4,060 on Friday, caught between margin-call selling and rate-hike reinforcement from the hot jobs data. The metal dropped despite Thursday's equity crash, as investors liquidated gold positions to cover losses elsewhere. Goldman Sachs cut its year-end 2026 target from $4,650 to $4,150, citing the hawkish Fed path. However, central banks bought 321 tonnes in Q3 — up 42% year-over-year — providing structural support. Gold still gained 4.6% on the week as the net safe-haven bid outweighed Friday's reversal.

watchItems.title: Oil's wildest week since COVID: Brent loses 13%
watchItems.text: Brent crude ended the week at $98.32 — essentially flat on Friday — but down 13% from Monday's $113 level, its steepest weekly decline since March 2020. The week encapsulated the market's whiplash: an 8.7% crash on Wednesday after the Democratic midterm sweep raised peace hopes, a 3.9% rebound on Thursday following tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, and a quiet Friday consolidation. Eurasia Group's 10% peace odds and 60% probability of renewed US strikes keep the geopolitical premium elevated, but the sheer scale of the midterm-driven selloff exposed how much risk premium was built into crude.

watchItems.title: Tech rebounds from worst day since 2020 — but correction territory holds
watchItems.text: The Nasdaq Composite rallied 1.1% on Friday, led by a 3.5% chip-sector bounce, partially recovering from Thursday's 6.4% crash — the worst day since March 2020. The VIX fell 9% to 25.6 but remains elevated. Asian markets absorbed the aftershock: South Korea's Kospi fell 6% and Japan's Nikkei shed nearly 6%. On the week, the Nasdaq dropped 3.4% and remains in correction territory. The AI regulation narrative from the Democratic sweep continues to weigh. Oracle fell after Microsoft ended an AI cloud rental deal.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: Down from $4,110 Thu · Goldman cuts year-end target to $4,150 · still +4.6% on week
desk.sum: Gold fell 0.9% to approximately $4,060 per ounce on Friday as the blowout jobs report (+165K vs 65K consensus) reinforced December rate-hike expectations and triggered margin-call selling. Goldman Sachs cut its year-end 2026 gold target from $4,650 to $4,150. Despite Friday's drop, gold gained 4.6% on the week as Thursday's safe-haven bid during the tech crash more than offset the reversal. Central banks bought 321 tonnes in Q3, up 42% year-over-year, providing structural support. The CME FedWatch probability of a December hike holds near 78%.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: Down from $52.40 · gold-silver ratio widens to ~78.2 · +5.8% on week
desk.sum: Silver slipped 0.8% to approximately $51.90 per ounce on Friday, tracking gold's decline following the hot jobs data. The gold-silver ratio held near 78.2. Despite the daily setback, silver posted a strong 5.8% weekly gain, supported by the dollar's mid-week weakness and safe-haven flows during Thursday's tech crash. Industrial demand from solar panel manufacturing and electronics continues to underpin the long-term outlook. The weaker dollar partially offset rate-hike headwinds.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $91 · −13% on week, worst since Mar 2020 · tanker attacks vs midterm peace hopes
desk.sum: Brent held essentially flat at $98.32 on Friday, consolidating after the wildest week since March 2020. The week's narrative: an 8.7% crash on Wednesday after the Democratic midterm sweep raised Iran peace hopes, followed by a 3.9% rebound on Thursday when tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz dashed those hopes. WTI settled at $90.83. On the week, Brent fell 13% from Monday's $113 — its steepest weekly drop since COVID. Eurasia Group maintains only a 10% chance of a negotiated resolution and a 60% probability of renewed US strikes. OPEC+ holds December quotas unchanged ahead of the November 29 meeting.

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME ~$14,000/t · bounced modestly from tech crash · Chile output at 2-decade low
desk.sum: Copper edged up 0.14% to approximately $6.35 per pound (about $14,000 per tonne) on Friday, stabilising after Thursday's risk-off selloff. The modest bid came as tech stocks staged a partial recovery and the dollar's post-NFP strength proved modest. Chile's Q3 copper output remains at its lowest in at least two decades, providing fundamental support. Shanghai spot premiums remain elevated amid tightening Chinese inventories. Copper fell about 3.8% on the week.

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Eased from $144 · still elevated on Hormuz supply concerns · YTD +27%
desk.sum: Newcastle coal eased slightly to approximately $143 per tonne on Friday, giving back a fraction of Thursday's gain as the Hormuz situation stabilised somewhat. Coal-to-gas switching economics continue to favour coal in Asia with LNG prices elevated above $34/MMBtu for December delivery. Year-to-date gains sit at approximately 27%. The market remains highly sensitive to shifts in the Iran diplomatic outlook, as any resolution would ease energy supply concerns and weigh on coal demand.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Best weekly gain since Aug at +8% · auto catalyst + hydrogen demand underpins
desk.sum: Platinum surged 1.1% to approximately $1,538 per ounce on Friday, capping its best weekly gain since August at nearly 8%. The metal benefited from a combination of safe-haven inflows, the WPIC supply deficit narrative, and a recovery in auto-sector sentiment after Thursday's broad selloff. Platinum's dual role as both a precious and industrial metal worked in its favour this week, capturing gold's safe-haven bid while its hydrogen electrolysis growth story attracted fresh buying. Support at $1,500; resistance at $1,560.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Recovered from $982 Thu low · still pressured by NMC-to-LFP battery shift
desk.sum: Palladium eased slightly to approximately $1,023 on Friday, consolidating after a partial recovery from Thursday's selloff to $982. Despite the daily dip, palladium gained nearly 5% on the week. The metal's heavily industrial demand profile (85%+ from auto catalysts) continues to leave it vulnerable to EV-transition concerns, as battery EVs require no catalytic converter. Nornickel's plant overhaul provides some supply-side support. The strong NFP data eased some auto-sector growth fears.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: 5+ tankers hit Thu · Eurasia Group: 10% peace odds · 60% chance of US strikes
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz remains at critical risk levels. Thursday's tanker attacks — at least five vessels and a tugboat hit — erased the brief diplomatic optimism triggered by the Democratic midterm sweep on Tuesday. Eurasia Group holds its odds of a negotiated settlement at just 10%, with a 60% probability of renewed US military strikes. The UK's UKMTO confirmed separate tanker incidents near Qatar. Tanker attacks in October reached 35 — close to a record — and most ships now refuse to report incidents. Iran's Supreme Leader has rejected any diplomatic accommodation. The Iran war has cost US households nearly $2,000 each in higher energy costs, according to Fortune.

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: Down ~10% m/m · US harvest nearing completion · managed money net short
desk.sum: December corn eased to approximately 439¢ per bushel on Friday, slipping modestly as the stronger dollar post-NFP weighed on US export competitiveness. The US corn harvest is nearing completion with yields largely meeting expectations. Managed money remains net short. The hot jobs report and resulting dollar strength partially offset the weaker macroeconomic backdrop from Thursday's equity crash. Brazil's safrinha planting progress is on track.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Down ~16% m/m · global supply ample · Russian exports resume
desk.sum: December wheat fell to approximately 587¢ per bushel, dropping 1.2% as ample global supply and the stronger post-NFP dollar weighed on prices. Resumed Russian grain shipments from Azov ports continue to cap rallies. Record managed-money short positions and adequate world stocks limit upside. The USDA's next WASDE report will provide updated supply-demand projections. Global wheat production is tracking near record levels for 2026/27.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: Down ~6% m/m · harvest pressure · Brazilian planting progresses
desk.sum: Soybeans fell to approximately 1,167¢ per bushel, down about 1.1%, pressured by the stronger dollar and continued harvest pressure. Soybean futures have reached recent lows as harvest-season selling intensifies and South American planting progresses on schedule. Chinese buying interest remains muted despite the potential for improved US-China trade relations under the incoming Democratic Congress. Goldman Sachs notes the global soybean balance remains comfortable.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH ~$2,300 · stabilised after $1B liquidation · Fear & Greed at 34
desk.sum: Bitcoin stabilised near $75,943 on Friday — roughly flat — after Thursday's brutal $1 billion liquidation cascade. The crypto market found a tentative floor as the Nasdaq staged a partial recovery, but sentiment remains fragile with the Fear and Greed Index at 34 (Fear). BTC is approximately 40% below its all-time high of $126,080. Ethereum held near $2,300. Spot Bitcoin ETFs saw modest inflows but insufficient to offset the macro headwinds. The strong NFP data and resulting rate-hike reinforcement added marginal pressure. MicroStrategy and Coinbase partially recovered from Thursday's 9–13% drops.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM ~$34 Dec delivery · TTF $34 · HH $2.90 · approaching winter demand
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) rose to approximately $34 per MMBtu for December delivery, up from the low-$32 range a week ago, as winter demand approaches and Hormuz uncertainty persists. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends to at least end-December 2026, with 38 cargoes (about 5 bcm) suspended since April. European TTF holds near $34/MBtu. Henry Hub firmed to $2.90. Natural gas rose 2% on Friday. The approaching Northern Hemisphere winter and tight LNG supply from the Qatar disruption support prices.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait $765 · tanker attacks maintain supply squeeze · Hormuz risk persists
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated with CFR Southeast Asia around $1,200 per tonne. Despite brief peace optimism from the midterm results, Thursday's tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz reinforced the acute supply squeeze in fertiliser and mining supply chains. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). The Democratic sweep may open new diplomatic channels, but Eurasia Group's 10% peace odds suggest little near-term relief. Chinese domestic sulfur holds near 7,200 yuan per tonne.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · supply steady
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds near $367 per tonne, largely unchanged. BPC's India contract at $383 per tonne CFR remains approximately $35 above China's 2026 benchmark. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions. The potential for improved US-China relations under the Democratic sweep may facilitate broader fertiliser market flows, but near-term supply-demand dynamics remain stable.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: Recovering from ¥90k low · price centre rising · Document No. 46 constraining supply
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) has risen to approximately 93,500 yuan per tonne, recovering from the 90,000-yuan consolidation lows. SMM reports the price centre is continuing to move higher as smelters hold prices firm amid loss-making pressure from raw-material cost inversions. Supply remains constrained under Document No. 46 export controls. The range has narrowed to 92,000–95,000 yuan per tonne. Downstream restocking ahead of the peak season supports marginal demand.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · China 98% of supply · Document No. 46 choking flows
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, up over 130% since early 2025. China's Document No. 46 export controls retain a presumption of denial for US end users, and the Busan truce's Document No. 72 suspension has not meaningfully restored exports. China produces about 98% of global gallium. The incoming Democratic Congress may pursue a different approach to US-China strategic mineral relations, but near-term supply dynamics are unchanged. The chip-sector turmoil adds demand uncertainty.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Down from $5.44 in 2024 · steel demand soft · VRFB adoption uncertain
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds near $5.02 per pound, soft as steel demand weakens amid the global risk-off environment. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but the timing of large-scale adoption remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply. The strong US jobs data does little to shift vanadium's structural demand picture.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Fell below $5,100 — lowest since early July · ICE inventories at new 2.5-yr high
desk.sum: ICE cocoa fell below $5,100 per tonne for the first time since early July, settling near $5,080. The continued decline reflects persistent pressure from rising ICE warehouse inventories — now at a new 2.5-year high of 3,740,476 bags. A possible 42–50% drop in Ivory Coast's mid-crop adds a bearish undertone for the season ahead. However, StoneX projects 2026/27 global output could fall 9.6%, potentially turning the current surplus into a deficit. Demand destruction from high prices is evident in Q3 grindings data.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: DRC quotas 96,600 t/yr · flat on week · NMC-to-LFP shift continues
desk.sum: Cobalt holds at approximately $33,525 per tonne, flat on the week. The DRC (70% of global mine supply) maintains export quotas of 96,600 tonnes per year through 2027 to support prices, but the EV battery chemistry shift from NMC to LFP continues to structurally reduce cobalt demand. The broader risk-off environment adds marginal pressure. European cobalt has weakened on demand concerns according to Argus Media.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Futures ~¥94k · spot ~¥99k · lithium up 2% Fri · range ¥90k–110k
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate futures held near ¥94,000 per tonne, with spot around ¥99,350. Lithium rose approximately 2% on Friday, the largest gainer among commodities tracked. The market is finding a trading range of 90,000–110,000 yuan per tonne after halving from the mid-May peak above ¥200,000. Guangzhou Futures Exchange activity remains active. Goldman Sachs projects a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028, but near-term destocking is accelerating, providing some support.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), little changed. Southeast Asian supply remains tight with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Auto-sector demand remains solid despite the tech-sector turmoil, supported by replacement-tyre cycles. The strong US jobs data (+165K) eases some auto-sector growth concerns.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Eased from $90 · long-term ~$72/lb · 440+ reactors · Kazakhstan acid shortfalls
desk.sum: Uranium spot eased to approximately $86 per pound U₃O₈, down from the $90 level near the late-August six-month high. Over 440 reactors operate worldwide with 60+ under construction. The Sprott Physical Uranium Trust continues to absorb spot supply. Kazakhstan (43% of mine output) faces production shortfalls due to acid supply constraints and has cut 2026 output targets. Western utilities are locking in long-term contracts at $72/lb as energy security drives nuclear policy.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: China 60% mine · 90% processing · NdPr prices declined Nov 3
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide trades near $75 per kilogram. Prices declined on November 3 according to Rare Earth Exchanges, while dysprosium and terbium quotations held steady. China controls about 60% of global mine output and over 90% of processing. Western premiums for heavy rare earths remain elevated. MP Materials (Mountain Pass) and Lynas remain the only significant non-Chinese producers. The Democratic sweep may shift the US approach to strategic mineral sourcing.

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · CIF China flat
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand — every tonne of steel needs 6–9 kg. High-purity manganese sulfate for EV batteries is an emerging demand driver. Port Hedland and Durban logistics remain the key supply-chain bottlenecks.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: Gave back Thu's 2.8% bounce · Indonesia 67% mine · surplus persists
desk.sum: LME nickel fell approximately 2.7% to about $15,875 per tonne on Friday, giving back Thursday's short-covering bounce as the stronger dollar and risk-off sentiment weighed. Indonesia's dominance at 67% of global mine output and continued NPI/HPAL expansions keep the market in surplus. Zinc's 2% drop on the day contributed to broader base-metals weakness. The strong US jobs data and rising rate-hike expectations add headwinds for industrial metals.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: Near 6-month low · Myanmar ban · Indonesia curbs · semiconductor demand intact
desk.sum: LME tin trades near $47,500 per tonne, holding at the lower end of its recent range near six-month lows. The correction from October highs near $53,000 continues despite structural supply constraints: Myanmar's Wa State mining ban removed roughly 10% of global supply, and Indonesia continues to tighten export licensing. Semiconductor and solder demand keeps the market structurally tight. LME tin stocks remain near historic lows.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: Pulled back from 4-year highs · TCs deeply negative · smelter cuts continue
desk.sum: LME zinc fell 2.1% to approximately $3,717 per tonne on Friday, pulling back from its recent four-year highs as the stronger dollar and risk-off mood triggered profit-taking. Treatment charges remain deeply negative, meaning miners effectively pay smelters to process concentrate. Several Chinese and European smelters have cut output. LME inventories have plummeted approximately 64% year-to-date. The fundamental picture remains tight despite the daily pullback.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: China raises H1 Nov contract prices · +200%+ since early 2026 · supply crisis deepens
desk.sum: Ammonium paratungstate (APT) prices continue to surge, with Chinese domestic long-term contracts raised to 550,000 yuan per tonne for the first half of November — up 50,000 yuan from the second half of October. Overseas APT holds above $3,300 per mtu. China's export controls on tungsten processing technology have created a severe non-Chinese supply crisis, with Western prices nearly quadrupling China's domestic levels. China produces about 79% of global tungsten and controls most processing.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: US+Qatar 81% · BLM reserve depleted · Hormuz threatens Qatar supply
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels as structural supply constraints tighten. The US BLM Federal Helium Reserve was fully depleted and privatised, removing the global buffer stock. Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium. Thursday's tanker attacks and Eurasia Group's 10% peace odds underscore the continued threat to Qatar's Ras Laffan output (25%+ of world supply). Semiconductor fabs, MRI machines and space launch consume most demand.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · irreplaceable in agriculture
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade and holding 70% of known reserves. DAP (diammonium phosphate) prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. Phosphate is irreplaceable in agriculture — every crop needs it, and there is no synthetic substitute. China periodically restricts fertiliser exports to protect domestic supply, creating price spikes.
